beef-steak-t-bone-lean-and-fat-eaten.title: Beef, T‑bone steak, lean and fat portions

content.title: About
content.content: The T‑bone steak is a large cut taken from the short loin of beef, containing both the tenderloin (lean side) and the strip loin (fat side) separated by a T‑shaped bone. This combination gives a juicy, flavorful eating experience that is prized for grilling and pan‑searing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the T‑shaped bone that divides the two meat sections.
In the United States T‑bone steaks are a staple on steak‑house menus, often served medium‑rare to keep the meat tender.
The fat side melts during cooking, basting the lean meat and adding a distinctive beefy aroma.
T‑bone is versatile: it can be grilled, broiled, pan‑seared, or smoked.
In Japan a similar cut is called “T‑bone” and is sometimes served lightly seared as a beef sashimi style.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: The heme iron in beef is highly bioavailable, and zinc supports immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins source
items.content: T‑bone steak is abundant in vitamin B12, crucial for nerve health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The marbled fat contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that, in moderation, support heart health.

items.title: Contains creatine and carnosine
items.content: These compounds help replenish muscle energy stores and act as antioxidants.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake of fatty beef cuts can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens such as E. coli or salmonella.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Beef is rich in purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: For the best texture, cook the T‑bone to medium‑rare (internal temperature about 55 °C). Let the steak rest 5‑10 minutes after cooking, then slice against the grain. Serve with grilled vegetables, mashed potatoes, or a simple butter‑herb sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh T‑bone steak in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped tightly in plastic film or a sealed container. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag. Thaw in the fridge for 12‑24 hours before cooking.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-fried-co.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs that are deep‑fried after being coated are a popular dish in many cuisines. The skin and coating are removed before serving, leaving tender, protein‑rich meat with a lower fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried chicken pieces are commonly served as snacks in bars and fast‑food restaurants.
The coating is usually made from wheat flour, spices and sometimes breadcrumbs, giving a crisp crust.
Removing skin and coating reduces the calorie count by roughly 30 %.
Chicken is classified as “white” meat, which is generally easier to digest than red meat.
In some countries fried chicken is accompanied by yogurt‑based or tomato‑based sauces.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of skin‑less fried chicken provides about 25 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin and coating cuts saturated fat, making the product more suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken contains niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Chicken protein has a high biological value, making it a good choice for people with increased protein needs.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Frying often involves added salt and sauces, which can raise sodium intake and affect blood pressure.

items.title: Trans fats in coating
items.content: If the coating is prepared with partially hydrogenated oils, trans fats may form, which are undesirable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Quality of frying oil
items.content: Reusing oil repeatedly can generate harmful compounds; it is advisable to change the oil after several batches.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fried chicken hot as a main dish or with side dishes such as mashed potatoes, rice, or vegetable salads. Pair with sauces like barbecue, mustard, yogurt‑based dip, or spicy chili.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked meat to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Latte is an espresso‑based drink made with a generous amount of steamed milk. In the nonfat version, skim milk is used, reducing calories and fat while preserving the creamy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Latte comes from the Italian word “latte,” which means “milk.”
Skim milk contains about ten times less fat than whole milk.
Latte is often decorated with milk‑foam designs known as latte art.
In the United States, latte is the most popular coffee drink in chain cafés.
Caffeine content in a latte depends on the espresso shots, typically 30‑60 mg per serving.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using skim milk lowers the overall calorie count, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Even skim milk supplies calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine may slightly increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can raise stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Milk allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance should choose alternative milks.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Pre‑made lattes may contain sugar, flavorings, or preservatives, increasing the calorie load.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Latte can be served hot or cold (iced latte). Drink it fresh, optionally adding cinnamon, vanilla, or a small amount of sweetener to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared latte is best consumed within 2‑3 hours. If refrigerated, use within 24 hours and gently reheat before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled ginger root is thinly sliced fresh ginger that has been cured in a vinegar brine with sugar, salt and spices. It has a bright aroma, a mildly sweet‑sour taste and a crunchy texture. It is commonly used in Asian cuisine, especially with sushi, rolls, salads and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled ginger, known as “gari” in Japan, is traditionally served with sushi to cleanse the palate between different pieces.
Ginger contains gingerol, the compound responsible for its characteristic pungent flavor and anti‑inflammatory properties.
The Japanese word “gari” literally means “pickled ginger”.
Pickling extends the shelf life of ginger, allowing it to retain its flavor and crunch for several months.
Ginger has been used in traditional medicine worldwide as a remedy for nausea and colds.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger stimulates gastric secretions and speeds up digestion, helping to reduce bloating.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effect
items.content: Gingerol and shogaol exhibit anti‑inflammatory activity, which may help lessen joint discomfort.

items.title: Reduces nausea
items.content: Ginger is widely used to alleviate nausea, including motion sickness and morning sickness.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phenolic compounds in ginger combat free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: B‑vitamins and vitamin C in ginger contribute to a stronger immune system.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to ginger, manifested as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Large amounts of ginger can cause heartburn or irritation of the stomach lining in people with high acidity.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Ginger may enhance the effects of anticoagulants such as warfarin, so intake should be limited when using these medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled ginger is served in small portions alongside sushi, rolls, salads or as a snack. It can be added to Asian sauces, marinades, rice salads, or used as a fragrant garnish for fish and seafood dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pickled ginger in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. When stored properly it retains its flavor and crunch for up to 6 months. Discard if you notice mold, discoloration or an off‑smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Ground ham (680) is a ready‑to‑use product made from selected pork meat that has been cooked and finely minced to a uniform texture. It has a mild, slightly salty flavor and a soft consistency, ideal for sandwiches, salads, casseroles, and hot dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground ham is widely used around the world as a quick source of protein.
During production small amounts of nitrites are added to preserve the pink color and extend shelf life.
Ham can be made from whole muscle cuts or a blend of trimmings, affecting taste and texture.
Thermal processing makes the product safe to eat without further cooking.
Ham is a common topping for pizza, omelets, and rolls.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Ham provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamins B1, B2, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals help maintain immune function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports thyroid health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites, which may be undesirable in large amounts.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may be allergic or intolerant to pork.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ham is relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham can be eaten straight from the package, added to sandwiches, salads, pastas, casseroles, omelets, and soups. It is also used as a filling for rolls and pizza. If desired, briefly warm it in a pan or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ham in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, keep it for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Discard any product with off‑odors or discoloration.

infant-formula-organic-powder-made-with-.title: Infant Formula Organic Powder (Made with Water)

content.title: About
content.content: Organic infant formula in powder form is designed to be prepared with water. It contains carefully selected ingredients such as whole cow's milk, plant proteins, vitamins and minerals that meet infants' nutritional needs. The product is certified to international quality standards and contains no GMOs, artificial colors or flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is made from organic ingredients grown without synthetic pesticides.
Each batch undergoes strict microbiological testing.
Developed according to WHO and national pediatric guidelines.
Packaged in recyclable material to reduce environmental impact.
The powder dissolves easily in water, creating a smooth, nutritious feed.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: A balanced mix of proteins, fats and carbohydrates provides essential amino acids and energy for rapid infant growth.

items.title: Rich source of vitamins and minerals
items.content: Includes vitamin D, calcium, iron and zinc, which support bone development, immunity and nervous system function.

items.title: Promotes digestive health
items.content: Contains pre‑biotics and probiotics that foster a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low allergen profile
items.content: Free from soy, gluten and lactose in free form, making the formula more hypoallergenic.

items.title: Environmental friendliness
items.content: Organic production reduces environmental impact and preserves biodiversity.

items.title: Cow's milk protein allergy
items.content: Children with known cow's milk allergy should consult a pediatrician before use.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: Follow the recommended water‑to‑powder ratio to avoid hyper‑ or hypoglycemia.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: After opening, keep the container in a dry place and use within the indicated period.

items.title: Water quality control
items.content: Use safe drinking water for preparation to prevent microbial contamination.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Measure the specified amount of powder, add it to boiled (or cooled to 40 °C) water, stir thoroughly until fully dissolved. Allow the mixture to cool to body temperature before feeding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, seal tightly. Discard the product if it develops an off‑odor, color change, or clumps.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is whole corn kernels that explode when heated, creating light, airy pieces. Ready‑to‑eat kettle popcorn is popped in oil with salt and flavorings, then sealed in an airtight package.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn has been enjoyed since ancient times; archaeologists have found popcorn remnants in Mayan tombs.
Each kernel contains about 14 % water; when heated, the water turns to steam and forces the kernel to pop.
Kettle popcorn is cooked in large kettles where kernels are constantly stirred in oil, giving a uniform flavor and crunchy texture.
Popcorn is one of the most popular cinema snacks; in the United States more than 13 billion servings are consumed each year.
There are over 30 flavor varieties, including caramel, cheese, barbecue, chili, and more.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Popcorn provides about 380 kcal per 100 g, which is lower than most crackers and chips when prepared with modest amounts of salt and oil.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in popcorn supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in corn have antioxidant properties that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Kettle popcorn often contains a notable amount of salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: Excessive oil increases the product’s calorie density.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Fine popcorn pieces can be inhaled, especially by young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn is convenient to eat straight from the bag as a quick snack. It can also be tossed into salads, soups, or used as a crunchy base for sweet treats like caramel popcorn.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator, and keep opened bags in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Porcupine balls are small dough pieces shaped into spiky spheres and served with a fragrant tomato‑based sauce. The dough is typically made from wheat flour, eggs, and spices, while the sauce combines ripe tomatoes, garlic, basil, and olive oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “porcupine balls” comes from their appearance: after frying they develop a golden crust that looks like a porcupine’s quills.
The tomato sauce follows a classic Italian recipe that slowly simmers tomatoes to deepen flavor.
The dish is popular in vegetarian menus, though it can be adapted with meat mince for a non‑vegetarian version.
Porcupine balls are often served as appetizers at buffets and family dinners.
In some regions they are finished with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: The dough provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour supply vitamins B1, B2 and B6, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain the antioxidant lycopene, which supports heart and skin health.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the sauce adds monounsaturated fats beneficial for blood vessels.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour adds dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour dough can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce is often salty; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich due to dough and oil, so moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: The dough contains eggs, which may be problematic for egg‑allergic individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the porcupine balls hot, drizzled with tomato sauce. They are easy to pick up with a fork or toothpick as a snack. Optional toppings include grated cheese, fresh basil, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked balls in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving to restore the crisp crust. Store the sauce separately in the fridge for up to 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran layer and germ. Combined with a mix of vegetables it creates a nutritious dish rich in fiber, vitamins, and minerals. It is commonly used in diet plans and Asian‑style meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice keeps more nutrients than white rice because the outer layers are intact.
It has a lower glycemic index, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.
There are over 40 varieties of brown rice, each with distinct flavor and texture.
Originally cultivated in Asia, brown rice is now grown in the United States, Europe, and Africa.
When stored properly in a cool, dry place, brown rice can last up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nervous system health, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3, and B6 aid in converting food into energy and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps control blood glucose levels, beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in brown rice protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like many grains, brown rice can contain trace amounts of arsenic; rinsing and cooking in excess water reduces exposure.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid may hinder mineral absorption; soaking before cooking lowers its level.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to rice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the rice by boiling, steaming, or using a rice cooker. Mix with broccoli, carrots, bell peppers, peas, or spinach. Add soy sauce, ginger, garlic, or lemon juice for flavor. Serve as a side, in salads, or as a warm main dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to slow fat oxidation. It typically stays fresh for 6–12 months.

rice-white-with-vegetables-and-gravy-ns-.title: Rice, white, with vegetables and gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, with vegetables and gravy is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of steamed white rice, a mix of fresh vegetables (carrot, peas, corn, bell pepper) and a flavorful gravy made from tomatoes and spices. The dish provides carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals and a moderate amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is commonly served in cafeterias and fast‑food outlets as a quick, nutritious meal.
Combining rice with vegetables supplies a complete set of amino acids and dietary fiber.
The gravy can be tomato‑based or cream‑based depending on the recipe.
White rice is cooked until tender but not mushy to preserve grain structure.
Vegetables are often steamed, retaining bright colour and nutrients.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a rapid source of energy thanks to its complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as potassium and magnesium, supporting overall health.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: The vegetables and a modest amount of whole‑grain rice increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Low saturated fat
items.content: The dish contains a small amount of fat, mostly polyunsaturated, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The gravy contributes water content, helping maintain proper hydration.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables or spices used in the gravy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravy can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in diabetics.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: The dish is calorie‑dense due to carbohydrates, so portion size should be managed, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main meal or as a side to meat or fish dishes. It reheats well in a microwave or on the stovetop, and fresh herbs can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C for up to 3 days. For freezing, place in an airtight container and store up to 2 months. Before eating, heat to at least 75 °C.
